query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) can reliably capture time‐dependent phase formation and oxidation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) by detecting transient oxide phases and structural changes during heating.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) in its as-cast state with a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA sample to high-temperature conditions (in air and/or vacuum) while continuously monitoring its structure using in situ HTXRD.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments (e.g., temperatures ranging from several hundred°C up to 800°C or higher), under controlled atmosphere conditions (vacuum or ambient air) to study oxidation kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of transient oxide phases (e.g., spinel or halite oxides mainly from Mn oxidation) that mediate the structural changes during the oxidation process.
generation.mechanism: HTXRD captures time–temperature-dependent diffraction peaks that indicate the onset and evolution of oxide formation and phase transformations, allowing correlations between oxidation behavior and phase stability to be directly observed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Distinct shifts in diffraction patterns and emergence of new peaks corresponding to oxide phases will be observed, confirming that high-temperature oxidation leads to measurable structural changes in the HEA.
generation.baseline: Traditional ex situ analysis methods that miss transient phases due to post-mortem sample preparation may fail to capture the real-time evolution of oxidation and phase transformations.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of in situ HTXRD may be limited in environments with rapidly fluctuating temperatures or in alloys with extremely complex oxidation kinetics beyond the resolution of the technique.
generation.uncertainty: Further validation is needed to determine if the findings generalize across different HEA compositions and complex industrial oxidation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of high-temperature oxidation experiments on CrMnFeCoNi HEA using in situ HTXRD, and simultaneously perform complementary ex situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses on quenched samples to verify phase formations. Compare the timing and extent of phase transitions detected by both methods.
measurements: Time-resolved XRD diffraction patterns during heating
Quantitative phase analysis from diffraction peak intensities
TEM imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) of quenched samples
Weight change measurements to correlate oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase evolution and oxidation kinetics identified by in situ HTXRD do not correlate (within acceptable experimental error) with the ex situ TEM/SAED analyses and oxidation mass gain measurements, then the hypothesis that in situ HTXRD reliably captures high-temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability in HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
